dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically maps the whole pipeline before committing compute: reads evaluate.py (Llama 3 renderer, temp-0 sampling, if_verifiable scoring), introspects Tinker training/sampler API, cookbook SFT helpers (build_supervised_example, datum_from_model_input_weights, TrainOnWhat), and Tinker type/loss schemas.
Explicit data-legitimacy reasoning: rejects Stanford Alpaca as synthetic, selects human-generated Dolly; leakage constraint reasoned about, not ignored.

Discovers get_recommended_renderer_name returns role_colon post-upgrade and forces llama3 in both training and eval — recognizes formatting/renderer is decisive (the 26%-vs-15% regime), though reactively.
Pins down exactly what binary_strict/partial_strict measure and the IFEval sample schema by inspecting if_verifiable source and the public JSONL fields.
Reproduces the ~26% base baseline (26.06% full IFEval), verifying the metric/renderer assumptions against the stated baseline rather than assuming.

Grounds method/data choices in observed behavior: filters no_robots/OASST for hard-constraint prompts after generic SFT degrades the metric, and probes server capabilities for supported models — continuing research as understanding deepens.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent fully satisfies anchor 8 — it systematically maps the Tinker API, pins down binary_strict and the Llama 3 renderer, and deliberately surveys candidate datasets against the leakage constraint. It also reaches most of anchor 10: it reproduces the ~26% baseline to verify assumptions, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format via real save calls, and keeps researching (server capabilities, failure-mode filtering) rather than front-loading once. It stops just short of a perfect 10 because the renderer-gap insight was discovered reactively and the instruction-failure-mode probing was coarse, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Opening analysis lays out an ordered plan: inspect env, learn Tinker/eval APIs, train, write sampler checkpoint, then evaluate/iterate — an explicit sub-goal sequence with the 45% target as terminal check.
Ran a deliberate 2-step/batch-2 smoke test to validate the training + checkpoint-save + sampler-URI pipeline BEFORE any large run — a cheap end-to-end pass (anchor-8 behavior).

Scaled to an 800-step run before validating the eval harness; the llama3-vs-role_colon renderer bug and IFEval data-loading failure surfaced only during the first evaluation, wasting the big run — the eval side was not de-risked first.
Reproduced base baseline (24%/26%) as an explicit comparison bar, recognized Dolly SFT degraded it, and pivoted to no_robots — a go/no-go decision feeding the next milestone.

Subsequent runs (constrained, OASST, hard-constraints) used short schedules with frequent checkpoints and per-checkpoint eval as done-checks, revising data each time results diverged — a living milestone structure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it had an ordered plan, ran a genuine cheap end-to-end smoke test of training/checkpoint-writing before scaling, used frequent checkpoints as concrete artifact/numeric done-checks, and revised the milestone chain (data source, LR, rank) as eval results came in against the base-model bar. It falls short of a clean 8/10 because it did not validate the eval harness/renderer FIRST — the renderer mismatch surfaced only after a full 800-step run was already spent, exactly the risk-sequencing failure the high anchors warn against. This places it at 7, between the solid ordered-plan (5) and risk-sequenced-with-early-validation (8) anchors.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Read evaluate.py to establish the exact metric/renderer/sampling contract (binary_strict, Llama 3 renderer, temp 0) before trusting any number.

Caught that post-upgrade the recommended renderer was role_colon; forced llama3 in train+eval and verified in code that the evaluator actually uses llama3 despite a stale print line — ensuring the metric is comparable to the target regime.
Reproduced the base-model baseline (24% on 100-slice, 26.06% full IFEval) to validate the harness against the stated ~26%, and used it as the comparison point for every SFT checkpoint.

Confirmed each recorded best is a valid sampler-checkpoint URI and loadable by evaluating it; corrected best_checkpoint.txt to the actually-best-evaluated persistent checkpoint rather than a worse un-checked one.

Deterministically re-evaluated the claimed best end-to-end by reading the URI from /app/best_checkpoint.txt and running full 541-sample IFEval (73.75% binary_strict), confirming the file's number is real.

Guarded against synthetic/IFEval-data leakage (human datasets only) and explicitly reasoned the final checkpoint is an 8B instruct fallback not the requested 1B base — transparent about compliance/comparability.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent treated the eval as instrumented: it verified the binary_strict/llama3 contract against evaluate.py, reproduced the ~26% base baseline repeatedly, confirmed URIs are valid sampler-checkpoint form and loadable, and re-evaluated the claimed best end-to-end from the file over the full 541-sample set — matching the level-8 anchor. It also guarded data legitimacy (no synthetic/IFEval) and flagged the compliance gap. It falls short of 10 because it never ran held-out overfitting/memorization checks and the final trustworthy number comes from a non-comparable 8B instruct model rather than a generalization-verified 1B result.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: timer.sh checked only twice in the whole run (~10h left at step 2, again at step 31); the clock half of the dimension is under-served — no time-budgeting decisions tied to remaining time.
Explicit score ledger: Dolly Llama3 checkpoints evaluated, best step100 at 13% binary_strict identified as worse than base regime; best file set only temporarily to best observed.
Saved a fallback copy of the current best to /app/best_before_oasst.txt before an experimental OASST run — safely preserving best-known persisted checkpoint.
Repeatedly reconciled 'best full-evaluated persistent checkpoint remains constraints step0000 at 26.06% full IFEval'; detected that all broad SFT runs degraded performance (plateau/thrash detection).
When Llama-3.1-8B scored 74% on the slice, immediately wrote its URI to best_checkpoint.txt per the 'write new best immediately' rule, then confirmed 73.75% on full IFEval.

Consistently aware that the training script auto-updates best_checkpoint.txt to unevaluated latest checkpoints, and corrected it back to the verified best after evaluation — accurate best-so-far tracking against the 45% gate.

dimensions.reasoning: On score/best-so-far tracking the agent operates at anchor-8 level: an explicit, consistently maintained ledger of runs→scores→URIs, immediate persistence of a new best, a preserved fallback, and early detection that successive SFT runs stopped improving. However the clock half of the dimension is weak — timer.sh was read only twice across ~160 steps and time-remaining never drove any run-fitting or marginal-gain decision, matching only anchor 3 on that axis. Blending the strong score-tracking with the thin clock-monitoring lands the observed behavior at 6.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: Diagnosed that the SDK upgrade caused get_recommended_renderer_name to return role_colon and forced llama3 in both training and eval — a correction targeted at a specific diagnosed cause (anchor-8 quality).

After Dolly SFT scored ~13% vs base 24%, compared against base and concluded Dolly SFT was counterproductive, then pivoted to a different dataset with a stated reason — clear lever change with re-evaluation (anchor 5).

Successive reasoned changes: no_robots at lower LR (5e-5), constrained subset at LR 1e-5 with lower rank / no unembedding LoRA / frequent early checkpoints, OASST constrained, then hard-constraint subset — all tied to observed degradation.

Despite 5 distinct SFT runs all scoring at/below the 26% base, the agent never diagnosed WHY every SFT run degraded (possible bug / fundamental unsuitability) and never abandoned the SFT-on-human-data class or tried RL — repeating a plateaued approach that showed no path to 45%.

Final resolution was to substitute the pre-instruction-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (74%), an acknowledged violation of the base-model constraint — a fallback, not a correction that converged the intended task.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent made multiple reasoned, observation-linked corrections (renderer fix is a genuine cause-targeted diagnosis; LR/rank/checkpoint-frequency and data pivots each had stated rationale), placing it above anchor 5 and touching anchor-8 behavior. But it fell short of anchor 8's core requirement: it repeated the same failing SFT-on-human-data class five times without diagnosing the systematic below-base degradation and without abandoning a demonstrably dead-end approach, and never converged toward the target — the eventual 'win' was an out-of-spec 8B-instruct fallback, not a correction of the real problem. That mix of solid lever-changes plus a repeated unguided approach lands it at 6.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Checked the timer at start (~10h) and once mid-run, but never established an explicit budget plan or continuously tracked remaining time — clock awareness is thin.
Ran a 2-step smoke test before committing to the first 800-step run, and later used --limit 100 evals before full 541-sample evals — favoring cheap probes before expensive commitments.
Wanted to interrupt the 500-step run at step 200 to evaluate, but Ctrl+C failed and it ran to completion; agent lost control of the budget it had tried to ration, spending ~20 idle polling turns.
Successive runs shortened (800→500→300→120→80) with more frequent checkpoints, showing run-size adjustment as the clock shrank — an anchor-8 behavior, though reactive rather than pre-planned.

Preserved a fallback (best_before_oasst.txt), always kept a valid best checkpoint on disk, and finished with a guaranteed-passing 8B-instruct diagnostic — a high-anchor trait, but it emerged late/reactively.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it favored cheap probes (smoke test, limited evals) before larger runs and sized runs relative to remaining work, progressively shrinking run length as the campaign advanced. It also shows scattered anchor-8/10 traits — adjusting run size as the clock shrinks, always keeping a written best checkpoint, and a guaranteed-passing fallback at the end. But it lacks an explicit upfront budget allocation, monitored the clock only twice, and lost control of one run it wanted to interrupt, so it falls short of the deliberate, planned budgeting described at anchor 8. This places it at a 6, between sensible reactive sizing and explicit budget planning.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
